description: We are JTK Relax from Bintulu, Sarawak, Malaysia—a creative team passionate about technology, storytelling and problem-solving.
summary: Echoes of Exploration is a short, caption-led illustrated video that brings three quiet NASA explorers into the spotlight: the Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle, Sojourner, and Opportunity. Through a young explorer’s journey across the Moon and Mars, the video shows what each machine was built to do, what it helped scientists discover, and how its mission ended. It highlights Apollo 15’s expanded lunar exploration, Sojourner’s role as the first rover on another planet, and Opportunity’s evidence that ancient Mars was once wet. Imagined dialogue gives each machine a voice, while on-screen facts keep the storytelling grounded in NASA sources. The project helps younger audiences connect engineering and space science with the stories behind the hardware left on other worlds. These machines may be silent, but their discoveries continue to shape exploration.
details:
1. Executive project overview

Echoes of Exploration is a mobile-first, illustrated educational experience for learners aged 10–14. Guided by a young explorer named Mira, players follow a mysterious fictional signal from an observatory to three historic exploration sites: Apollo 15 on the Moon, Mars Pathfinder and Sojourner, and the Opportunity rover at Meridiani Planum on Mars.

The experience combines short character-led narration, a clear six-screen journey, small tap-based interactions and concise mission fact cards. Its central idea is that exploration is cumulative: each mission expands what people can observe, test and understand about worlds beyond Earth.

PROJECT ELEMENT

DESIGN DEFINITION

Core format

Responsive web-based illustrated story with tap-to-continue narration and optional audio.

Primary audience

School-age learners aged 10–14; accessible to casual space enthusiasts.

Experience duration

Approximately 4–6 minutes for one complete journey.

Core journey

Six screens: title, signal map, Apollo 15, Sojourner, Opportunity, and closing map.

Learning approach

Story first, interaction second, verified mission facts clearly labelled and easy to revisit.

Prototype scope

Three mission artefacts, three simple interactions, three fact-card groups, captions and replay.

 

VALUE PROPOSITION

The project makes planetary exploration easier to understand by connecting real engineering and science achievements to a memorable story. It is designed to be small enough to complete, test and demonstrate as a working prototype.

 

2. Project rationale and objectives

The project is built around a simple learning challenge: mission names, dates and scientific findings can feel disconnected when presented only as facts. Echoes of Exploration gives each mission a role in one connected narrative, then uses fact cards to make the real science explicit.

2.1 Project objectives

·   Introduce three important milestones in space exploration through a coherent and age-appropriate story.

·   Explain the different purposes of a crewed lunar vehicle and two robotic Mars rovers.

·   Help learners understand how mobility, observation and evidence contribute to scientific discovery.

·   Encourage curiosity about engineering, planetary science and future exploration.

·   Demonstrate an accessible, mobile-friendly learning prototype that can be completed in a few minutes.

2.2 Intended learning outcomes

BY THE END OF THE EXPERIENCE, A LEARNER SHOULD BE ABLE TO…

EVIDENCE IN THE PROTOTYPE

Describe why Apollo 15 used a Lunar Roving Vehicle.

Moon scene and route-tracing activity; Apollo 15 fact card.

Explain how Sojourner reached the Martian surface.

Pathfinder lander/ramp interaction and Sojourner fact card.

State what Opportunity helped scientists learn about ancient Mars.

Rock-clue interaction and ancient-water fact card.

Distinguish a fictional storytelling voice from historical mission information.

Explicit “imagined story voice” label and separate verified fact cards.

Recall one unique contribution made by each mission.

Three-marker closing map and mission-facts review option.

 

2.3 Audience and learning level

The primary audience is learners aged 10–14. Use short sentences, familiar vocabulary and one main idea per narration segment. Introduce technical terms only when they are explained in context. The experience should not assume prior knowledge of the Apollo programme, Mars exploration or planetary geology.

3. Experience design principles

PRINCIPLE

HOW IT SHOULD APPEAR IN THE PRODUCT

Story-led, fact-checked

Mira and the machine voices create emotional connection; dates, distances and discoveries remain in separate fact cards.

One clear action per screen

Each scene presents one primary action, such as tracing a route, deploying a rover or inspecting a rock.

Mobile-first

Large touch targets, concise text, vertical scrolling only when necessary and responsive layouts.

Learning by doing

Interactions reveal an idea or piece of evidence; they are not decorative taps without educational value.

Accessible by default

Captions, optional sound, readable contrast, keyboard support and reduced-motion options.

Respectful science storytelling

No invented NASA quotations, fabricated mission recordings, crashes or false claims of live signals.

 

4. User journey and screen architecture

The prototype is intentionally limited to six screens. The map is the navigation anchor: it introduces the journey and returns at the end, showing how the three mission stories connect.

SCREEN

PURPOSE

PRIMARY USER ACTION

SYSTEM RESPONSE

01 · Title

Set the tone and explain the experience.

Select “Begin the journey”.

Open the signal map; offer a short text description of the artwork.

02 · Signal map

Orient the learner to the Moon and Mars.

Select the Moon marker.

Transition to the Apollo 15 scene; show progress.

03 · Apollo 15

Explain how the lunar rover extended astronaut fieldwork.

Trace a short route or select sample marker.

Reveal route completion, samples icon and Apollo 15 fact card.

04 · Pathfinder / Sojourner

Show how a lander delivered a mobile rover.

Select the ramp, then inspect a nearby rock.

Play a short deployment animation and reveal the “look closer” panel.

05 · Opportunity

Connect long-duration exploration with evidence of ancient water.

Inspect a rock, then select “What happened?”.

Reveal the water clue and explain the 2018 dust storm.

06 · The echoes continue

Consolidate the learning and invite another exploration.

Review mission facts or restart.

Return to the illuminated Moon-and-Mars map; show credits and sources.

 

RECOMMENDED NAVIGATION

Show a simple progress indicator (for example, “3 of 6”) and a persistent home/map control. Avoid a complex branching map in the first prototype; the intended experience is short and linear.

 

5. Screen-by-screen storyboard

5.1 Screen 01 — Title screen

Visual direction: A calm, deep-space star field. Place the project title prominently, with three faint silhouettes representing the lunar rover, Sojourner and Opportunity. Keep the interface uncluttered and ensure the main button is immediately visible.

On-screen copy: “Echoes of Exploration” / “An interactive story about the machines that helped us explore the Moon and Mars.” / Primary button: “Begin the journey”.

Interaction: The primary button opens the signal map. Provide a short text alternative describing the artwork. Audio must not autoplay.

5.2 Screen 02 — The signal map

Visual direction: An illustrated Moon-and-Mars map against a star field. Three points of light mark the featured artefacts. A dotted trail leads from Mira’s observatory to the first destination.

On-screen copy: “Three echoes detected. Follow the trail.”

Interaction: The learner selects the Moon marker to begin. The same map returns at the ending with all three markers illuminated.

5.3 Screen 03 — Apollo 15 landing site

Visual direction: A wide lunar panorama inspired by the Apollo 15 landing area. Show the Lunar Module and Lunar Roving Vehicle as historical artefacts. Do not animate the real rover as though it is operating today.

On-screen content: Mira’s dialogue with the Lunar Roving Vehicle, followed by a clearly labelled fact card: first Apollo mission to use the Lunar Roving Vehicle; approximately 17.5 miles travelled; more than 170 pounds of lunar samples collected.

Interaction: The learner traces a simple route between two or three points. On completion, reveal a sample icon and the mission fact card. A tap alternative must be available for anyone unable to drag or trace.

5.4 Screen 04 — Pathfinder and Sojourner

Visual direction: Warm rust-red Martian terrain, the Pathfinder lander, a visible deployment ramp, Sojourner and a small group of nearby rocks. Make the rover’s small scale understandable without making it look like a toy.

On-screen content: Mira’s dialogue with Sojourner and a fact card explaining that Pathfinder demonstrated a way to land on Mars and deploy the first rover to explore the planet’s surface.

Interaction: Selecting the ramp triggers a short, simple deployment animation. The learner then selects a nearby rock to open a “Look closer” panel explaining that Sojourner examined Martian rocks and soil.

5.5 Screen 05 — Opportunity’s landscape

Visual direction: A quiet plain at Meridiani Planum. Show Opportunity beside a rock. After the dialogue, a subtle dust haze gradually increases. Avoid crash imagery, a dramatic shutdown animation or a fabricated final transmission.

On-screen content: Mira’s dialogue with Opportunity. The fact card should state that the rover was designed for about 90 Martian days, operated for almost 15 years, and stopped communicating during a severe Mars-wide dust storm in June 2018.

Interaction: Selecting a rock reveals a simple before-and-after illustration: evidence of ancient water in the rocks, contrasted with the cold, dry landscape seen today. The “What happened?” control explains the dust storm and distinguishes the last communication date from the later formal mission conclusion.

5.6 Screen 06 — The echoes continue

Visual direction: Return to the Moon-and-Mars map. Illuminate all three markers. Mira’s notebook displays three sketches: a lunar rover track, a deployment ramp and a rock. Reuse the flower symbol as a small visual signature, not as a substitute for the project title.

On-screen content: Closing narration and the statement “Their machines are quiet now. Their discoveries are not.” Add “Explore mission facts again” and “Start the journey over” controls. Include a sources and credits link.

Interaction: The fact-review option opens a concise three-mission summary. Restart returns to the title screen or signal map, depending on the chosen build flow.

6. Refined story script

SCRIPTING NOTE

All dialogue spoken by the Lunar Roving Vehicle, Sojourner and Opportunity is original, imagined storytelling. It is not a real recording, transcript or quotation from NASA or mission personnel. Keep this distinction visible in the interface.

 

Opening — The signal

Setting: Mira stands at a small observatory after sunset. A soft, fictional signal draws a glowing dotted trail across a map of the Moon and Mars. A small flower icon appears beside a rover silhouette.

NARRATOR  “Some explorers return home. Others leave their footprints far beyond Earth.”

MIRA  “If nobody is there to hear them… can their stories still reach us?”

SIGNAL  “Three echoes detected. Follow the trail.”

NARRATOR  “Mira opens her notebook. Her first destination: the Moon.”

Player action: Select the Moon marker. Provide persistent captions and a “Skip narration” control.

Fact note: The signal is a fictional framing device. It does not suggest that NASA received a real signal.

Scene 1 — The Moon roadster

Setting: Apollo 15 landing site, 1971. Mira sees the Lunar Roving Vehicle parked near the lunar module. The rover is shown as a historical artefact, not as a vehicle operating in the present.

MIRA  “You helped astronauts travel farther across the Moon.”

LUNAR ROVING VEHICLE  “I was designed to carry astronauts, tools and scientific equipment across the lunar surface. On Apollo 15, David Scott and James Irwin drove me during their exploration.”

MIRA  “What did that extra distance make possible?”

LUNAR ROVING VEHICLE  “The crew could examine more of the landscape, compare rocks and collect more samples. My wheels helped turn a distant place into a field site.”

NARRATOR  “Before leaving the Moon, the astronauts parked the rover near the lunar module. Their samples and observations travelled home with them.”

Player action: Trace a short route on a simple map. Reveal the sample icon and fact card when the route is completed.

Fact card: Apollo 15 was the first mission to use the Lunar Roving Vehicle. The crew travelled approximately 17.5 miles (27.9 kilometres) in it and collected more than 170 pounds of lunar samples. The rover remains at the Apollo 15 site.

 

Scene 2 — The little trailblazer

Setting: Mars Pathfinder landing site, 1997. Mira follows a trail of small wheel marks to Sojourner beside the Pathfinder lander. A visible ramp connects the lander to the Martian surface.

MIRA  “You look small beside the lander.”

SOJOURNER  “I travelled to Mars with Pathfinder. After landing, I rolled down a ramp and became the first robotic rover to explore the surface of another planet.”

MIRA  “What could a little rover teach us?”

SOJOURNER  “I could move close to rocks, examine rocks and soil, take pictures and send observations back to Earth. My mission showed how a lander could deliver a mobile robot to Mars.”

NARRATOR  “Sojourner’s journey was small in distance, but large in what it made possible for the robotic explorers that followed.”

Player action: Select the ramp to deploy Sojourner, then select a nearby rock to reveal a “Look closer” panel.

Fact card: Mars Pathfinder landed on 4 July 1997 and demonstrated a way to land safely on Mars and deploy the Sojourner rover to the surface.

Scene 3 — The long-distance explorer

Setting: Meridiani Planum on Mars, during Opportunity’s final mission period. The landscape is wide and quiet. Opportunity stands beside a rock. A dust haze slowly grows after the dialogue.

MIRA  “Your mission was supposed to be short, wasn’t it?”

OPPORTUNITY  “My planned mission was about 90 Martian days. I kept exploring for almost 15 years.”

MIRA  “What did all that time help scientists discover?”

OPPORTUNITY  “I studied rocks that showed liquid water had changed this region long ago. Those clues helped scientists understand that ancient Mars once had environments that may have been suitable for life.”

NARRATOR  “In June 2018, a severe Mars-wide dust storm reduced the sunlight reaching Opportunity’s solar panels. The rover stopped communicating with Earth.”

MIRA  “Your signal went quiet. But the clues you found are still helping us ask new questions.”

Player action: Select a rock to reveal the ancient-water clue. Then select “What happened?” to reveal the dust-storm explanation.

Fact card: Opportunity operated for almost 15 years, far beyond its planned 90-Martian-day mission. Its last communication was received on 10 June 2018 during a severe Mars-wide dust storm. NASA declared the mission complete on 13 February 2019. Opportunity’s observations provided evidence that parts of Mars were once wet and may have been habitable.

Ending — The echoes continue

MIRA  “One rover helped astronauts explore farther. One showed that a robot could explore another planet. One kept searching for clues long after its first plan.”

NARRATOR  “Their machines are quiet now. Their discoveries are not.”

MIRA  “What story will the next explorers find?”

ON-SCREEN MESSAGE  “Exploration leaves questions behind. The next generation can follow them.”

Player action: Offer “Explore mission facts again” and “Start the journey over”. Include sources and credits.

Fact note: The ending is an original summary of the three missions, not a NASA quotation.

7. Interaction and learning mechanics

INTERACTION

LEARNING PURPOSE

RECOMMENDED BEHAVIOUR

ACCESSIBLE ALTERNATIVE

Apollo 15 route trace

Connect mobility with broader surface exploration and sample collection.

Learner traces a short, simplified route. Completion reveals sample marker and fact card.

Select ordered route points using taps or keyboard; do not require dragging.

Sojourner ramp deployment

Show how the rover was delivered from the lander to Mars.

Tap the ramp; play a brief 2D deployment animation; then enable rock selection.

Provide “Deploy rover” button; animation can be skipped.

Rock inspection

Introduce observation as a scientific method.

Tap a rock; open a short “Look closer” panel with one image and one explanatory sentence.

Focusable labelled button with text description.

Opportunity water clue

Help learners connect rock evidence to ancient environmental conditions.

Tap the rock; transition to a clear before/after or evidence overlay.

Static side-by-side image and explanatory text.

Dust-storm reveal

Explain why Opportunity stopped communicating without inventing a dramatic ending.

“What happened?” reveals the dust storm, last contact date and mission-end date.

Text disclosure control; avoid time-limited or audio-only information.

 

7.1 Interaction design rules

·   Every interactive element must have a clear label and a visible response.

·   Use one primary action per screen; secondary actions should not compete with it.

·   Allow learners to continue without audio and to revisit fact cards without replaying the full story.

·   Use short animations to explain a process, not to simulate unverified mission events.

·   Keep progress and navigation consistent across all six screens.

8. Visual, audio and accessibility specification

8.1 Visual direction

ELEMENT

RECOMMENDED DIRECTION

Overall identity

A cinematic but calm space-science visual language: deep navy, muted teal, warm gold highlights and restrained star-field details.

Moon scene

Low-saturation grey lunar terrain, strong silhouette separation and clear scale cues for the lander and rover.

Mars scenes

Distinct rust-red environments; use visual composition to differentiate Pathfinder’s compact landing area from Opportunity’s broad plain.

Typography

Use a highly legible sans-serif typeface. Keep dialogue short and avoid placing text over visually busy terrain.

Buttons and controls

Consistent shape, strong contrast, clear labels and generous spacing. The primary action should be visually dominant.

Illustration integrity

Use original artwork or correctly credited NASA media. Label conceptual artwork; never present generated illustrations as actual mission photographs.

 

8.2 Audio and narration

·   Use gentle radio static only at the opening, followed by subtle ambient tones; keep sound secondary to the story.

·   Provide captions for every spoken line and a visible “Skip narration” or “Continue” control.

·   Do not autoplay audio. Offer mute and volume controls where audio is included.

·   Use distinct but restrained voices: Mira is curious and warm; machine voices are calm and reflective.

·   All dialogue must remain understandable when audio is muted.

8.3 Accessibility requirements

·   Provide persistent captions and text alternatives for meaningful artwork.

·   Maintain readable text size, strong text/background contrast and sufficient spacing.

·   Do not communicate information by colour alone; pair colour with labels, icons or patterns.

·   Support keyboard navigation and visible focus states for buttons and interactive objects.

·   Use sufficiently large touch targets and avoid interactions that require precise dragging.

·   Offer reduced-motion behaviour or a way to skip animations; avoid flashing effects.

·   Use semantic headings, labelled controls and descriptive alternative text for screen readers.

9. Scientific accuracy and content governance

The educational credibility of the project depends on a visible boundary between storytelling and evidence. The fictional signal and machine dialogue are creative devices. Mission dates, measurements, discoveries and mission status must be checked against authoritative sources and presented as factual information.

CONTENT TYPE

RULE

EXAMPLE

Creative narrative

May use personification, emotion and metaphor, but must be labelled as imagined dialogue.

“My wheels helped turn a distant landscape into a field site.”

Mission fact

Must be concise, specific and traceable to a source.

Apollo 15 travelled approximately 17.5 miles in the Lunar Roving Vehicle.

Mission status

Use precise dates and distinguish last contact from formal mission closure.

Opportunity last communicated on 10 June 2018; NASA declared the mission complete on 13 February 2019.

Artwork

Identify conceptual scenes and credit NASA/JPL imagery or other assets as required.

“Illustrative reconstruction; not an actual mission photograph.”

 

ACCURACY CONTROL

Do not state that Opportunity’s mission officially ended in June 2018. June 2018 marks the last communication; NASA announced the mission’s completion in February 2019.

 

10. Recommended prototype implementation

The following is a practical implementation recommendation for the first demonstrable build. It does not assume that the software has already been developed or that a particular technology stack has been selected.

AREA

RECOMMENDED APPROACH

WHY IT FITS THE SCOPE

Delivery

Responsive web experience that runs in a modern mobile and desktop browser.

Easy to access during a presentation without app installation.

Structure

Six-screen linear flow with reusable scene, dialogue and fact-card components.

Keeps the prototype manageable and consistent.

Interaction

Lightweight JavaScript interactions with CSS/SVG or simple 2D animation.

Sufficient for route tracing, ramp deployment and rock inspection.

Media

Optimised illustrations, optional compressed narration and captions.

Supports loading performance and silent use.

Content

Mission facts stored separately from story dialogue.

Makes fact-checking and future revision easier.

Data and privacy

No account or personal information required for the prototype. Avoid collecting identifiable learner data.

Appropriate for a short educational experience for minors.

Resilience

Provide a clear restart path and graceful behaviour if audio is unavailable.

Prevents a missing asset or muted device from blocking learning.

 

10.1 Core build components

·   Screen controller: manages the six-screen sequence and return-to-map behaviour.

·   Dialogue component: presents speaker names, short text chunks, captions and optional narration.

·   Fact-card component: displays verified facts, source attribution and a close/review action.

·   Interaction layer: route selection, rover deployment and rock-clue reveal.

·   Accessibility layer: keyboard focus, text alternatives, reduced motion and audio controls.

·   Credits and source panel: lists NASA mission pages and image credits used in the final build.

11. Scope, deliverables and acceptance criteria

11.1 Minimum viable prototype

MUST INCLUDE

NOT REQUIRED FOR THE FIRST PROTOTYPE

Six complete screens and three mission artefacts.

A free-roaming 3D solar-system environment.

Opening, three mission scenes and closing script.

Additional missions beyond Apollo 15, Sojourner and Opportunity.

Three meaningful interactions and three fact-card groups.

Complex physics simulation or high-fidelity rover controls.

Captions, skip/continue controls and restart/review flow.

User accounts, profiles or personal data collection.

Mobile-responsive layout and source/credit panel.

Live feeds, live NASA telemetry or external real-time mission connections.

 

11.2 Acceptance criteria

·   All six screens can be completed in the intended sequence without dead ends.

·   Each of the three featured artefacts has one working interaction tied to its learning point.

·   Every factual statement is supported by a NASA or JPL source in the source register.

·   All spoken content is available as captions; the story remains usable with audio off.

·   The layout is usable on a typical smartphone screen and a desktop browser.

·   The learner can review the three mission summaries and restart the experience.

·   No artwork is misrepresented as a real NASA photograph and no imagined line is presented as a historical quotation.

12. Team workflow and responsibilities

WORKSTREAM

KEY RESPONSIBILITIES

OUTPUT

Research and fact-checking

Verify mission dates, distances, discoveries, status and approved imagery. Maintain the source register.

Fact cards and source/credit list.

Script and narration

Refine the language for ages 10–14, manage pacing and record optional narration.

Final script, captions and audio files.

Illustration and interface

Create scene assets, icons, layout, buttons and visual consistency.

Six screen designs and optimised assets.

Prototype development

Assemble navigation, interactions, fact cards, accessibility and responsive behaviour.

Working web prototype.

Testing and presentation

Run learner usability checks, resolve issues and prepare the demonstration.

Test notes, final pitch and demo flow.

 

12.1 Suggested delivery sequence

1.  Lock the facts and approve the script before recording audio or finalising artwork.

2.  Create low-fidelity layouts for all six screens and confirm the main action on each screen.

3.  Build the complete linear journey with placeholder art and working interactions.

4.  Replace placeholders with final illustrations, captions, narration and source credits.

5.  Test on a phone and desktop; fix navigation, readability, interaction and accessibility issues.

6.  Prepare a short live demonstration using the finished six-screen journey.

12.2 Prototype testing plan

Recommended test group: a small supervised group of representative learners in the target age range, plus at least one adult reviewer for clarity and accessibility. Obtain any required school or guardian permission before involving minors. The first test should focus on comprehension and usability, not on collecting personal information.

TEST QUESTION

WHAT TO OBSERVE

SUGGESTED SUCCESS SIGNAL

Can learners follow the story?

Where they pause, backtrack or ask what to do next.

Most testers complete the six screens without facilitator help.

Do interactions make sense?

Whether route, ramp and rock actions are discoverable.

Each primary action is completed without guessing.

Do the facts stick?

Ask learners to describe one contribution from each mission.

Learners can explain the three missions in their own words.

Is the content accessible?

Try with audio muted, keyboard only and a small screen.

Core content and actions remain available in each mode.

Is the experience well paced?

Measure total time and note screens that feel too slow or dense.

Typical completion falls within the intended 4–6 minute range.

 

The success signals above are proposed validation targets, not existing test results. Record actual observations before making claims about learning impact or usability.

13. Key risks and mitigation

RISK

POTENTIAL IMPACT

MITIGATION

Story voice mistaken for a real NASA transcript

Misrepresentation of historical evidence.

Label all machine dialogue as imagined; keep fact cards visually separate.

Incorrect or oversimplified mission facts

Loss of educational credibility.

Use NASA/JPL primary references; maintain a fact-check register and review dates/units.

Overambitious prototype scope

Incomplete screens or unreliable demonstration.

Keep the first build to six screens, three artefacts and three interactions.

Small text or unclear controls on mobile

Learners struggle to follow the experience.

Test on real phone screens; use short text blocks and large labelled controls.

Audio unavailable or muted

Narrative becomes inaccessible.

Persistent captions and text-first interaction flow.

Generated art mistaken for archival imagery

Confusion about what is historical.

Label conceptual art; use credited mission media only where reuse is permitted.

Excessive animation or effects

Distraction, motion discomfort or slower loading.

Keep animation restrained, optional and easy to skip.

 

14. Competition presentation narrative

14.1 Suggested 60–90 second project pitch

PITCH

What if the machines that explored the Moon and Mars could tell us what they discovered? Echoes of Exploration is a short, interactive learning journey for young space enthusiasts. Guided by Mira, learners follow a fictional signal to three real milestones: Apollo 15’s Lunar Roving Vehicle, the Sojourner rover delivered by Mars Pathfinder, and Opportunity, which explored Mars for almost 15 years. Instead of asking learners to memorise mission facts, the experience lets them trace a lunar route, deploy a rover from a lander and inspect a rock for clues of ancient water. Every machine voice is clearly presented as imaginative storytelling, while dates, discoveries and mission records appear in verified NASA fact cards. Designed as a six-screen, mobile-friendly prototype, the project makes planetary exploration approachable, memorable and easy to share. The machines are quiet now — but their discoveries continue to inspire the next generation.

 

14.2 What makes the project distinctive

·   One connected narrative links a human lunar mission with two robotic Mars exploration milestones.

·   The interactions are directly tied to scientific ideas: mobility, deployment and evidence from rocks.

·   The experience is short and focused, making it suitable for a classroom introduction or public demonstration.

·   The creative narrative is transparent about what is imagined and what is verified.
